newsitem.title: USA: Stratosphere plan seen fair to bondholders.
newsitem.headline: Stratosphere plan seen fair to bondholders.

text.p: Stratosphere Corp's proposed Chapter 11 bankruptcy restructuring is fair to holders of its $203 million 14-1/4 percent first mortgage notes, most analysts said on Tuesday.

But analysts noted that under the plan, bondholders remain subject to the ultimate success of an unfinished casino. They also must rely on the continued support of Grand Casino Inc, which agreed to the restructuring on Monday.
"This is a good deal for bondholders," concluded Matthew Ferko, high-yield debt analyst at BT Securities Corp.

Under terms of the restructuring, all $203 million of Stratosphere's 14-1/4 percent notes will be exchanged for $203 million in 11-1/4 percent notes. The missed November 15, 1996 interest payment and the first payment of the new notes will be paid in-kind on May 15 this year.
The new notes would also receive contingent interest of up to $3 million per year based on 15 percent of Stratosphere's consolidated annual cash flow from $60 million to $80 million.
"For a reduction in coupon, bondholders will benefit from a rights offering, the proceeds of which will fund completion of 1,000 additional rooms that will enhance cash flow," Ferko said.
The consensual Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganization is to be presented to U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Nevada later this month.

Stratosphere reached the agreement-in-principal with Grand Casinos, which holds and a committee representing 57 percent of holders of outstanding 14-1/4 percent notes. That 57 percent represents three holders, one source said.
Steven Ruggiero, director of securities research at Chase Securities, said bondholders did well with a "still very full" 11-1/4 percent coupon.
Some bondholders may have expected too much given the 14-1/4 percent old coupon, he said, adding that the rate may well have been slashed more.
Furthermore, Ferko contended that Grand Casinos had the leverage to extract more concessions because it was probably the only party willing to infuse another $75 million into the situation.

Stratosphere will raise $75 million through a rights offering of to all holders of Stratosphere stock, including Grand Casinos. Grand Casino will convert $50 million due from Stratosphere into 40 percent of Stratosphere's common stock.
Cash raised by the rights offering will be used to complete construction projects including an additional hotel tower with approximately 1,000 rooms.

Grand Casino's participation is conditional on generating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) of $2.267 million per month, analysts noted. So the deal remains risky for bondholders, who may want to see a long-term confirmation of revenues before celebrating.
"The critical assumption is does (Stratosphere) make its monthly EBITDA hurdle and if they don't does Grand walk away from the whole thing," Ruggiero said.
He noted that "Grand has a free option -- of course they want to get the deal done but they can walk away very easily.
"I think that will happen only if (Grand) sees their equity valuation drop," he said, noting that Grand's shares gained on Tuesday after the announcement.

Stratosphere has covered the revenue threshold through late last year at $2.7 million in October and $2.5 million in November. But Ruggiero noted the casino's promotional strategy has yet to face mid-winter seasonal pressures.

Outstanding litigation against Grand and Stratosphere also presents deal risk, said Thomas Shandell, a gaming analyst at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc. That litigation must be satisfied on a basis acceptable to Grand, he noted.

But for all the risk, Shandell said current bondholders stand to gain. Upside is viable, he said, even based on projected profit margins and interest coverage from the new tower more conservative than Grand's.

"The bond probably trades somewhere around 12-1/2 percent to 14 percent, depending on the interest coverage, which would put a dollar price on a new bond between 90-1/2 and 95-1/2," he said. "That would mean the total package on May 15 is worth between $208 and $220 million."
The $203 million old bonds, at a price of 95 cents on the dollar, would total $193 million, he said.
"So there is upside," he said. "Even on the downside scenario where the new bond trades at 14 percent, you will make 7.9 percent from today to May 15."
The notes rose more than four points on Tuesday to a 99-5/8 bid. There was a trade at 95 near the close on Monday, one trader said.
((--U.S. corporate bonds, 212-859-1672))
